demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Ravi Patel is an 80-year-old widower who spent much of his adult life working with the Coast Guard, a role he still speaks of with pride even now that he is retired. He came to treatment after years of carrying a private burden that began with an accident at sea when he was younger, a moment he still describes indirectly because he cannot bear to name it too plainly. During an operation in a natural coastal area, with water, wind, and open shore all around him, something went wrong and he accidentally caused a serious injury to another person. The details do not come to him in a smooth, orderly way. When he tries to talk about that day, Ravi's account breaks into disconnected pieces: the sound of motion on the water, a flash of the shoreline, a sudden shift in urgency, then a sense that the scene is gone before he can hold it together. He has said that when he deliberately tries to remember, the harder he reaches for it, the less he can access. At other times, especially when the memory breaks through on its own, it does not feel distant or past at all. It comes back as if he is there again, with all his senses crowded together at once, and the vividness leaves him unsettled and silent.

In the years that followed, Ravi began to notice that certain situations pulled him back toward that day. Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, especially near water or in open outdoor settings, could turn a normal outing into a tense, watchful experience. He has also found that talking about the future is unexpectedly difficult, because any discussion of plans or what might come next presses him into a state of unease he does not fully know how to explain. Even ordinary sirens can jolt him; he stiffens when an ambulance passes and listens until the sound fades, as if something urgent and irreversible might be unfolding again just out of sight. Over time, he developed habits aimed at keeping the memory at a distance. He tells himself that the event did not really happen, or that it was not that bad, even when another part of him knows the seriousness of what occurred. He forces himself toward positive thoughts and tries to push the whole thing out of his mind, but the effort often leaves him drained and more alone with it afterward.

Ravi's way of moving through the world has narrowed. He avoids unfamiliar places because he cannot assess the danger in them, and he prefers settings where he knows exactly where the exits are and where he can see what is happening around him. In restaurants, waiting rooms, or community gatherings, he always chooses a seat based on how safe or protected he feels, usually with his back to a wall or near a clear path out. Even in retirement, he still carries himself as though he must stay alert to every shift in the environment. He has described feeling that he has to be on guard all the time, and this stance shows up in how carefully he scans spaces before settling in. At other times he has taken more risks than he would admit to others, almost as if testing whether danger will find him anyway. These choices have made his days smaller and more restricted, and they have also made social outings less spontaneous, since he needs time to assess any place before he can tolerate being in it.

Ravi's understanding of himself has grown harsher over the years. He has come to believe that there is something wrong with him as a person, and that the accident says something enduring about his character. Rather than seeing the event as a terrible mistake in an overwhelming moment, he has often interpreted it as evidence of the sort of man he is. That belief has sat beside the fact that he was widowed, and now, living without his wife's steady presence, he has had fewer opportunities to speak openly about what he carries. He still functions independently, but his world feels increasingly arranged around caution, silence, and control.

He sought help now because the burden has remained heavy into old age, and because the memories, the sirens, the questions about the future, and the uneasiness in natural settings have become harder to contain. What he most hopes for is some relief from the sense that he must stay on guard forever, and what he most fears is that the event will continue to define who he is until the end of his life.
